front: Boss/workers vs pipeline (6 threads, 11 orders): which wins on average time to complete an order, and by how much?
back: The boss/workers model wins: 196ms vs 220ms for the pipeline.

front: Toy shop, 11 orders of 120ms, 6 threads per model: how are the boss/workers and pipeline averages derived?
back:
• Boss/workers: 1 boss + 5 workers, so waves of 5, 5, 1 finish at 120, 240, 360ms; average (120*5 + 240*5 + 360)/11 = 2160/11, about 196ms
  • Pipeline: 6 stages of 20ms; order k finishes at 120 + 20(k-1)ms; average 2420/11 = 220ms

front: Toy shop: who prefers the pipeline model and who prefers boss/workers, and why?
back:
• The manager prefers the pipeline: it completes more orders in a fixed time (better total execution time / throughput)
  • The customers prefer boss/workers: their individual orders come back sooner (lower average completion time)

front: Which Threading Model Is Better: what is the general takeaway about deciding between models?
back: You usually cannot declare one model universally better. Performance is relative to the metric being measured, and different metrics matter in different contexts. Change the number of workers or orders and you may draw the opposite conclusion.

front: "What is useful?" depends on the application. Match each example to the metric it cares about: matrix multiply, web server, hardware chip.
back:
• Matrix multiply: raw execution time
  • Web server: throughput (requests/time) or response time
  • Hardware chip: overall utilization

text: For any metric we may care about the {{c1::average}} value, the {{c2::max/min}} value, or the value at a certain {{c3::percentage}}, e.g. a task that completes in 3ms 95% of the time may be sufficient.
extra: Outliers can behave very differently from the rest, so an evaluation based on averages may look very different from one based on 95th percentile values.

front: Visual metaphor: give the toy shop and OS meaning of throughput, response time, and utilization.
back:
• Throughput: the manager wants as many orders completed as possible; OS: how many processes complete over a period of time on a platform
  • Response time: how long, on average, to react to a new order; OS: when we click the mouse, does something happen immediately or do we wait a noticeable amount of time
  • Utilization: what percentage of the workbenches is used over a period of time; OS: does the design use the CPU, devices and memory well, or leave a lot of resources unused

front: Define a performance metric.
back: A metric is a measurable or quantifiable property of a system that we are interested in, used to evaluate the system's behavior.

front: Performance Metrics: to compare implementations with a metric, over what should the metric be explored?
back: Over a range of meaningful parameters, for example by varying the workload or the resources allocated to the implementation.

front: Performance Metrics: name several useful metrics discussed.
back:
• Execution time
  • Throughput
  • Response time
  • CPU utilization
  • ...and many more

front: Performance Metrics: define wait time.
back: Wait time is when a job will start executing (not when it finishes). We usually want this to be low: wait as little as possible before jobs start.

front: Performance Metrics: why does low wait time matter for interactive jobs and for long-running jobs?
back:
• Interactive jobs: the user can start interacting sooner
  • Long-running jobs: the user finds out sooner that something is going wrong, and can stop the job, reconfigure it and launch it again

front: Performance Metrics: define throughput.
back: Throughput is how many tasks a platform completes in a given unit of time. It can be evaluated for a single server up to an entire datacenter.

front: Performance Metrics: what does platform efficiency measure and why does a datacenter owner care?
back: Platform efficiency measures how well resources are utilized to deliver a given throughput. The owner makes money from high throughput but spends money maintaining the platform; higher efficiency means spending less on the platform.

front: Performance Metrics: what metrics apply when you care about cost or energy?
back:
• Cost: performance per dollar
  • Energy: performance per watt, or performance per joule for energy over an execution
Used for purchase decisions: is the cost of the next hardware platform offset by a boost in performance per dollar; with high energy costs, the right purchase may be a more energy-efficient machine.

front: Performance Metrics: what is an SLA, and what does the percentage of SLA violations capture?
back: A Service Level Agreement is what enterprise applications typically give their customers, e.g. a response within three seconds, or (for a service like Expedia) the most accurate quote for 95% of the flights returned. The percentage of SLA violations captures how many requests took longer than promised or returned quotes that were not accurate.

front: Performance Metrics: give an example where maximizing a metric is NOT the goal.
back: Smooth video needs at least 30fps, since humans cannot perceive more than 30fps. Maximizing fps makes no sense; the goal is to make sure there are at least 30fps. This is client-perceived performance, not raw performance.

front: Performance Metrics: give an example of an aggregate metric.
back: Averaging the execution time or the wait time over all tasks, possibly weighted by the priorities of the tasks. You may need to aggregate metrics or even derive new ones to accurately understand a system.

text: The CPU is not the only resource we care about: metrics capturing average usage of {{c1::memory}}, of the {{c2::file system}}, or of the {{c3::storage subsystem}} are useful too.

front: Performance Metrics: define a testbed.
back: A testbed is the experimental setting: it tells us where/how the experiments were carried out and what relevant metrics were gathered.

front: Performance Metrics: ideally measurements come from what, and what is the fallback when that is infeasible?
back: Ideally: real software on real machines with real workloads. Fallback: representative "toy" experiments with similar access patterns and similar machines, optionally supplemented by simulation to mimic a larger system than we can build.

front: "Really, are threads useful?" What is the honest answer, and why is it unsatisfying?
back: The answer is "it depends": on the metrics gathered and on the workload. It is pretty much always the correct answer to a question in systems, but never an accepted one, including in this course.

front: "Is X useful?" depends on the workload: give the lecture's three examples.
back:
• Toy shop: boss/workers vs pipeline depended on the number of toy orders
  • Shortest path: some algorithms work best on sparsely connected graphs, others on densely connected ones
  • Filesystems: some are better for predominantly read accesses, others for a mixed workload where files are both read and updated

front: MP vs MT: what context does the lecture use to compare multiprocess and multithreaded implementations?
back: A web server, which wants to use concurrency to more efficiently process client requests. Both approaches provide concurrency.

front: Web server response flow: which steps are CPU-bound, network-bound, and disk-bound?
back:
• CPU: request parsing, header creation
  • Network: accepting a connection, reading the request, sending the data
  • Disk: finding and reading the file

front: Web server flow: do the network and disk steps always block?
back: No. They may block, depending on the state of the system at that moment: the connection may already be pending, or the file data may already be cached in memory from a previous request, in which case no device is involved and the step completes much more quickly.

front: Multiprocess web server: how is concurrency achieved and what is the main benefit?
back: Run multiple instances of the same process. Benefit: it is simple; once the app is correct, just spawn multiple processes.

front: Multiprocess web server: list the downsides.
back:
• Higher memory footprint
  • High cost of context switch between processes
  • Hard/costly to maintain shared state across processes (IPC constraints)
  • Hard to have multiple processes listen on a specific port

front: Multithreaded web server: how is concurrency achieved, and what patterns can be used?
back: Concurrency within a single address space. Each thread can do all steps, or use boss/workers (boss accepts connections, workers do the remaining steps, from reading the HTTP request to sending the file), or a pipeline where each thread does one step only.

front: Multithreaded web server: list the benefits.
back:
• Shared address space and shared state
  • Cheap user-level context switch
  • No system calls needed to coordinate (processes need them)
  • Lighter memory requirements from shared information

front: Multithreaded web server: list the downsides.
back:
• Not a simple implementation
  • Requires explicit application-level synchronization code, adding complexity
  • Depends on OS-level thread support (less of an issue today)

front: Event-driven model: describe its structure (address space, thread, core component).
back: Single address space, single thread of control. The core is an event dispatcher that loops looking for incoming events and invokes the registered handler(s) based on event type.

front: Event-driven web server: what do events correspond to?
back:
• Receipt of a request
  • Completion of a send
  • Completion of a disk read

front: Event-driven model: how does the dispatcher behave, and how is a handler invoked?
back: The dispatcher operates like a state machine. Since it is single-threaded, invoking a handler is just a function call: execution jumps to that instruction in the process's address space.

front: Event-driven web server: which handler does each event go to, from new connection to file sent?
back:
• Pending connection request on the server's port: accept connection handler
  • Message on an established connection: read request handler
  • File found: sent in chunks, iterating over the send handler as each chunk completes
  • File not there: an error message is sent to the client

front: Event-driven model: what rule do handlers follow, and what happens if a handler must block?
back: Handlers run to completion. If a handler needs to block (e.g. an I/O request), it initiates the blocking operation and immediately passes control back to the dispatch loop.

front: How does the event-driven model achieve concurrency, versus MP/MT?
back: MP/MT handle one request at a time per execution context, gaining concurrency from multiple contexts. The event-driven model interleaves the processing of multiple requests within a single execution context.

front: Event-driven concurrency example: C1's read file handler starts disk I/O, then C2 and C3 connect. What is each client doing some time later, and what does it show?
back:
• C1: sending its file in chunks, waiting between chunks
  • C2: waiting on disk I/O to read its file
  • C3: waiting on its HTTP message from the network
One thread of execution, yet multiple client requests are processed concurrently; their processing is just interleaved.

front: Event-driven model on a single CPU: how long is one request processed before switching to another, and why does this beat switching among threads when there is no idle time?
back: A request is processed exactly until a wait is necessary, then the execution context switches to servicing another request. If there is no idle time, context switching among threads just wastes cycles that could have been used for request processing.

front: Event-driven model with multiple CPUs: when does it still make sense, and what must be ensured?
back: It makes sense when there are more concurrent requests than CPUs: each CPU hosts one event-driven process serving many requests, with less overhead than context switching among processes/threads. Gotcha: you must steer the right events to the right CPU.

front: Event-driven model: how are network and disk represented, and what represents both?
back: The OS uses sockets as an abstraction over the network and files over the disk. Both are represented by file descriptors. An event is input on any file descriptor associated with the server.

front: Event-driven model: compare select, poll, and epoll for finding a ready file descriptor.
back:
• select: takes a range of FDs, returns the first with input
  • poll: an alternative to select
  • Both must scan a potentially large list of FDs, of which very few have input, so much of the search time is wasted
  • epoll: more recent (e.g. Linux), eliminates the scanning-large-lists problem; many high performance servers needing high data rates and low latency use it today

front: Event-driven model: where do its benefits (low overhead) come from?
back: From being a single address space with a single flow of control: smaller memory footprint, no context switching or synchronization, and simpler programming (no synchronization primitives or shared-variable reasoning).

front: Event-driven model: what is the locality downside, and how big is it?
back: Jumping among handlers for different connections hurts locality and pollutes the cache, but these effects are far smaller than the cost of a full context switch.

front: Event-driven model: what blocking problem does it share with the many-to-one ULT:KLT model?
back: If one handler initiates a blocking call, the entire process can be blocked, just as a blocking user-level thread blocks the whole process in the many-to-one model.

front: Helper threads/processes: what are asynchronous I/O operations and what do they require?
back: When the call is made, the kernel captures enough information about the caller and about where and how the data should be returned once it becomes available. The caller continues execution now and checks the results later; it is not blocked in the kernel while the I/O takes place. Made possible by a multithreaded kernel (another kernel thread does the waiting) and can also benefit from hardware devices that report a request's results later.

front: Why do asynchronous I/O operations fit nicely with the event-driven model?
back: Their completion events can be caught with the same select, poll or epoll mechanism the dispatcher already uses.

front: Helper threads/processes: when async I/O is unavailable, how do helpers fake it?
back: Async I/O is not available on all platforms or for all device types (e.g. an accelerator device only the server can access). Then a handler passes a potentially blocking I/O call to a helper and returns to the dispatcher. The helper does the blocking I/O; it blocks, but the main event loop does not. Communication uses sockets or pipes, which look like file descriptors so select/poll still work.

front: What do AMPED and AMTED stand for, and when is each used?
back: AMPED = Asymmetric Multi-Process Event-Driven: helpers are processes, needed when the kernel is not multithreaded (as back in the day). AMTED = Asymmetric Multi-Threaded Event-Driven, the multithreaded equivalent: helpers are threads; a follow-on to the Flash work implements it.

front: AMPED: in what sense are the processes asymmetric?
back: The helpers only deal with blocking I/O operations; the main process performs everything else.

front: AMPED: what are the key benefits over pure MP/MT and basic event-driven models?
back:
• Resolves portability issues of basic event-driven: fakes async I/O instead of requiring native support, and does not depend on kernel threading support
  • Smaller footprint: a helper does an isolated task, not all request-processing steps
  • Needs a helper only per concurrent blocking I/O operation, not per concurrent request

front: AMPED: list the downsides.
back:
• Works well for server-type applications, but is not necessarily applicable to arbitrary applications
  • Complexities around event routing on multi-CPU systems

front: Models and memory quiz: of boss/workers, pipeline and event-driven, which likely requires the least memory, and why?
back: The event-driven model. Its handlers are just procedures in the one address space; extra memory is needed only for the helpers of concurrent blocking I/O calls. Boss/workers needs a thread for every concurrent request; the pipeline needs multiple threads per stage once concurrency exceeds the number of pipeline stages.

front: Flash web server: what model does it follow and what blocking I/O does it deal with?
back: Flash is an event-driven AMPED web server with asymmetric helper processes. The blocking I/O operations are basically just disk reads.

front: Flash: how does the dispatcher decide between a local handler and a helper for a file?
back: The helper maps the file in memory with mmap; the dispatcher checks with mincore whether the pages are in memory. If the file is already in memory, reading will not block, so the local handler is used; otherwise a helper. Helpers report back to the dispatcher via pipes.

front: Flash: what does the mincore residency check cost, and why is it worth it?
back: It is extra work before every file read, but it yields big savings: it prevents the whole process from blocking when a blocking I/O operation turns out to be necessary.

front: Flash residency check: the lecture mentions mmap/mincore. What does Pai et al. say about the order and mechanism?
back: The residency check comes first: the main process tests mapped file pages with mincore() before use (Secs. 5.4, 5.7). Only if pages are not resident does it dispatch a helper; both the main process and helper mmap the file, the helper touches every page, then notifies the main process via IPC that the file can be sent without blocking (Sec. 3.4).

front: Flash: what application-level caching does it do, on what?
back: Caching at multiple levels, on both data and computation: cached files (data), cached pathname-to-file lookups (computation), and cached response headers (file-dependent, valid as long as the file is unchanged).

front: Flash: what networking optimizations does the lecture describe?
back:
• Data structures are aligned so DMA operations can be performed without copying data
  • DMA with scatter-gather: the header and the file data need not be next to each other in memory; they can be sent from different locations, avoiding a copy
Fairly common now, but novel when the paper was written; some of the compared systems did not include them.

front: Flash header padding: the lecture calls it a network hardware optimization. How does Pai et al. frame it?
back: As byte position alignment, not a network hardware feature (Sec. 5.5). When writev() sends a header then file data, the OS copies the regions into a contiguous kernel buffer; a header length not a multiple of the word size misaligns every subsequent copy. Flash pads headers to multiples of 32 bytes to target 32-byte cache lines; the section does not mention DMA.

front: Apache web server: what does the core provide and what do modules do?
back: The core provides the core server functionality: accepting connections and managing concurrency. Modules are mounted in a pipeline and extend the basic server behavior (e.g. security features, management of dynamic content, basic HTTP request processing); a deployment may contain one or more.

front: Apache: how is its flow of control similar to the event-driven model?
back: Each request passes through all the modules, much as a request passes through all the handlers in the event-driven model.

front: Apache: what concurrency model does it use?
back: A combination of multiprocess and multithreaded: each instance is a process implementing a multithreaded boss/workers configuration with a dynamic thread pool, grown or shrunk according to configurable thresholds. The number of processes is also adjusted dynamically, based on the number of outstanding connections, the number of pending requests and CPU usage.

front: Experimental methodology: what three questions must a good experimental design answer?
back:
• What systems are you comparing? (keep hardware fixed to compare software; keep software fixed to compare hardware)
  • What workloads will you use? (real-world vs dummy data)
  • How will you measure performance? (execution time, throughput, etc.; and for whom)

front: Flash experiments: why gather traces from real web servers and replay them?
back: A realistic sequence of requests captures a real distribution of web page accesses, and replaying the trace reproduces the experiment with the same pattern of accesses.

front: Flash paper: which five implementations did the authors compare?
back:
• Multiprocess, single-threaded (MP)
  • Multithreaded boss/workers (MT)
  • Single process event-driven (SPED)
  • Zeus (SPED with two processes; the second process deals with blocking I/O)
  • Apache (multiprocess at the time)

front: Flash experiments: all implementations except which one included Flash's optimizations, and what does that make the comparison?
back: All except Apache included Flash's optimizations. So the comparison is really between the models (MP, MT, SPED) and AMPED, over otherwise identical code.

front: MT architecture: lecture describes it as boss/workers. How does Pai et al. actually describe Flash-MT?
back: Each thread performs all steps of one HTTP request before accepting a new one, analogous to a process in MP (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 3). Flash-MT uses 64 threads and no boss thread is described (Sec. 6).

front: Zeus: lecture calls it a two-process SPED. What does Pai et al. clarify about its configuration?
back: Zeus v1.30 is a SPED server run as a single process for the synthetic-workload experiments and in a two-process configuration (vendor-advised) for the real-trace tests (Sec. 6). The two-process setup gives Zeus a slight edge over single-process Flash-SPED in trace tests, since one process keeps serving while the other blocks on disk I/O (Sec. 6.2).

front: Flash experiments: what two real-world traces were used and how do they differ?
back:
• CS WebServer trace: Rice University CS dept server; many files, does not fit in memory
  • Owlnet trace: student-run websites; much smaller, typically fits in a common server's memory

front: Flash experiments: why also use a synthetic workload generator in addition to real traces?
back: To run best-case and worst-case analysis and ask "what if" questions about access patterns they had not observed, rather than only replaying a real distribution.

front: Flash experiments: define the bandwidth metric.
back: Bandwidth = total bytes transferred divided by total time to transfer them.

front: Flash experiments: define the connection rate metric and why the authors cared about it.
back: Connection rate = total client connections serviced divided by total time elapsed. They cared because they wanted to see Flash's ability to perform concurrent processing.

front: Flash experiments: both metrics were evaluated as a function of file size. What is the expected effect of larger files on each?
back:
• Bandwidth: higher, because connection cost is amortized over more bytes
  • Connection rate: lower, because there is more work per connection

front: Flash best-case experiment: what workload defines the best case and why is it best?
back: A synthetic load where every request asks for the exact same file (requests varied in number). It is best because after the first request the file is cached, so subsequent requests are answered much faster.

front: Flash best case: what was varied, what was measured, and what shape do the curves have?
back: File size varied from 0 to 200 KB (varying the work per request); bandwidth measured as requests * file size / total time. All implementations rise sharply with file size, then plateau.

front: Flash best case: overall, how much did the choice of server architecture matter?
back: Little: all of the implementations had similar results.

front: Flash best-case results: rank the implementations and explain the top of the ranking.
back: SPED is best: no threads/processes to context switch among. Flash is similar but pays for its memory-presence check, which buys nothing here (same single file, no helper ever invoked). MT/MP are lower (synchronization and context switching). Apache is lowest (no optimizations).

front: Flash best case (lecture): what anomaly does Zeus show, and what causes it?
back: Its performance drops a little at larger file sizes (around 125KB in the graph), from a misalignment in some of its DMA operations: not all of Zeus's optimizations are bug free.

front: Flash best-case: lecture says Zeus drops in performance around 125KB due to DMA misalignment. What does Pai et al. actually say?
back: The paper discusses a Zeus anomaly only on FreeBSD, for file sizes between 10 and 100 KB, attributing it to the writev byte-alignment problem of Sec. 5.5 (Sec. 6.1, Fig. 7). The Solaris single-file graph (Fig. 6) the lecture shows is not discussed as a Zeus anomaly, so the ~125 KB figure is a reading of that graph, not the paper's stated result.

front: Flash best-case: lecture blames MT/MP's lag on synchronization and context switching. How does Pai et al. attribute it?
back: The paper attributes the slight lag of Flash-MT and Flash-MP to "extra kernel overhead (context switching, etc.)" and does not mention synchronization (Sec. 6.1). MP has private address spaces and needs no user-level synchronization between requests; only MT needs it for shared data, so synchronization is an MT-only cost.

front: Owlnet trace results: what is the ranking and why is Flash slightly above SPED?
back: Flash and SPED are best, then MT/MP, then Apache. The trace is small so most requests are served from cache, but some need blocking I/O: SPED blocks, Flash does not (it has helpers), so Flash edges out SPED. Zeus is not in this graph.

front: CS trace results: why does SPED's performance drop so much?
back: The CS trace is large so most requests are not served from cache. Since the system has no asynchronous I/O, SPED blocks on disk reads and falls from near-Flash to below both MP and MT.

front: CS trace results: why does MT beat MP, and why does Flash beat both?
back: MT beats MP: smaller memory footprint (more memory available to cache files), and it can synchronize more quickly/cheaply. Flash beats both: smaller footprint than MT/MP, so more memory for caching files and headers and fewer requests needing blocking I/O; everything is in one address space, so no explicit synchronization is needed.

front: Impact of optimizations: what are the four Flash curves compared?
back:
• Flash with no optimizations
  • Flash caching only the pathname lookup
  • Flash caching the pathname lookup and the file (via mmap)
  • Flash with all optimizations, adding cached header computation

front: Impact of optimizations: what trend do the curves show?
back: Connection rate decreases with file size in all cases, but increases as more optimizations are added; fully optimized Flash has the highest connection rate at a given file size. Apache lacked these optimizations and performed worst in both traces.

front: Summary of results: when data is in cache, how do SPED, AMPED Flash, and MT/MP compare?
back: SPED smokes AMPED Flash, because Flash makes an "unnecessary" memory-presence test per request. Both SPED and AMPED Flash beat MT/MP, since neither incurs synchronization or context-switching overhead.

front: Cached-data performance: lecture says SPED "smokes" Flash. How does Pai et al. phrase the SPED vs AMPED gap?
back: Flash-SPED only "slightly outperforms" Flash on the single-file test because of the residency check (Sec. 6.1), and on cached trace workloads Flash is "very competitive" with Flash-SPED, only a slight difference (Sec. 6.2). So SPED and AMPED are roughly tied on cached data.

front: Summary of results: when the workload is disk-bound, why does AMPED Flash beat SPED and MT/MP?
back: Beats SPED because SPED blocks on I/O (no async I/O), while Flash does not. Beats MT/MP because its efficient memory use leaves more memory for caching and it needs less context switching; only concurrent I/O-bound requests become extra processes/threads in AMPED.

front: Performance observation quiz: at about 100MB, Flash (AMPED) starts beating SPED. Which reasons apply: Flash handles I/O without blocking; SPED starts receiving more requests; the workload becomes I/O bound; Flash can cache more files?
back: Correct: Flash can handle I/O operations without blocking (helper processes), and the workload becomes I/O bound (beyond about 100MB it no longer fits in the cache as well), so a single blocking I/O blocks the entire SPED process and none of its other requests progress. Wrong: SPED does not get more requests (both get the same number); Flash cannot cache more files.

front: Performance quiz: does Flash's memory advantage explain why it beats SPED?
back: No. SPED and AMPED Flash have comparable memory footprints, so neither caches appreciably more files. If anything, Flash's helper processes take memory away, leaving Flash with less cache memory than SPED.

front: Summary: is the event-driven model suitable for every server, and how common is it?
back: No: you must route events to the right core on a multicore machine, and some processing does not fit the architecture. Still, many high-performance servers today are event-driven with asynchronous I/O support.

text: A well-designed experiment leads to statements about a solution that are {{c1::credible}}, so others believe them, and {{c2::relevant}}, so others care about them.
extra: Designing experiments takes more thought and planning than running test cases, gathering metrics and plotting results. The Flash paper is full of such experiments.

front: Designing experiments: web server clients vs operators, what metric does each care about?
back:
• Clients care about response time: how quickly they get a response
  • Operators care about throughput: how many client requests are served over a period of time

front: Designing experiments: must a solution improve both response time and throughput to be viable?
back: No. It may improve both, improve response time while keeping throughput constant, or improve response time while degrading throughput; any can be viable depending on the context (whose problem you are solving). E.g. better response time with worse throughput can pay off if it lets the operator charge clients more.

front: Designing experiments: besides comparing solutions, what experiment on load would the lecture also want for a web server?
back: Experiments that show how the response time clients see is affected as the load on the web server, the request rate, increases.

front: Designing experiments: what is the rule of thumb for picking metrics?
back: Start with metrics that are standard for the target domain (e.g. client request rate, server response time for web servers). This broadens your audience, so include them even if they are not the best punchline. Also pick metrics that answer the who/what/why.

front: Designing experiments: which metrics answer the who/why for clients, and which for operators?
back:
• Client performance: response time or the number of timed-out requests
  • Operator costs: throughput or power costs

front: Designing experiments: what system factors affect metrics?
back:
• System resources: CPU and memory configuration, software
  • Software resources: number of threads, queue sizes, buffer structures
  • Workload configuration: request rate, concurrent requests, file size, access pattern
The Flash experiments varied the request rate, the file size and the access pattern.

front: Designing experiments: what makes the ranges of varied parameters valid?
back: Pick the subset of configuration parameters most likely to affect the metrics, and make their ranges realistic: not 1, 2 or 3 threads when real setups use hundreds; file sizes from tens of bytes to hundreds of megabytes and beyond.

front: Designing experiments: is it acceptable to use configurations that are uncommon in practice?
back: Yes, for best/worst-case analysis, as long as they are still possible. The Flash single-file experiment is one of these, and it was still informative.

front: Designing experiments: how many experiments should confirm the same observation?
back: Pick useful combinations of the factors you vary: a few experiments confirming the same observation are good; tens of them are pointless.

front: Designing experiments: what is the "compare apples to apples" rule?
back: Only vary one parameter at a time. Do not run a large workload with few resources and then a small workload with more resources (say, more threads): if the second run is faster, you cannot tell whether the resources or the workload made the difference.

front: Designing experiments: what should you compare against for a baseline?
back: Show your experiment improves the state of the art or at least the most common configuration/workflow. Failing that, compare against extreme workloads or resource assignments to show how your solution scales.

front: Running experiments: what are the basic steps and the two reporting imperatives?
back: Steps: run test cases N times, compute metrics averaged over the N runs, and represent the results (a good visual strengthens the argument). Imperatives: do not just show results, draw a conclusion, spelling out what the results say about the hypothesis/claim.

front: Experimental design quiz: a toy shop with 3 shared working areas wants to know how many workers to hire for the worst case (trains). Which experiment answers it: (1) trains with 3, 4, 5 workers; (2) blocks/3, bears/6, trains/9; (3) mixed with 3, 6, 9; (4) trains with 3, 6, 9?
back: Configuration 4: the worst case (only trains) in every trial, adding an even number of workers per working area. (1) spreads workers unevenly over the 3 areas; (2) changes the toy type between trials, so it says nothing about worst-case capacity; (3) could show how average throughput on a mixed workload responds to more workers, which is not the manager's question.

front: Experimental design quiz: toy shop with 3 shared working areas, why are trials of 3, 6, 9 workers better than 3, 4, 5?
back: 3, 4, 5 workers do not spread evenly across the 3 areas, so resource-per-area differs across trials and differences say nothing about capacity. 3, 6, 9 add the same number of workers to every area, so the results reflect how capacity responds to more workers. Pushing to 12 (4 per area) reveals where gains flatten: the area's capacity.
